blocks.text: A chisel hits the workshop floor. Then the second one.
Two days since my first match. I came off that stand with four ring still in me, and my hands still won't close round a handle.
For most people that would be a nuisance. For a mason with the Guild bailiff knocking on my door, right now, it's the whole problem.
He knocks again. Four knocks, evenly spaced. Of course they are.
"Banker's grief," I tell the chisels, and leave them where they fell, which my master would have clouted me for. I open the door.
Same bailiff. Same grey coat. He glances at his own notice, still square on its four nails, as if checking I haven't shifted it in the night.
"Halloway."
"Other side," I say, because he's on my left. He steps round with the face of a man who suspects a trick.
"Midwinter Quarter Day," he says. "Thirty-eight crowns, to the Guild. I'm required to say it in person once the notice is up."
"You said it with nails. I thought it was very clear."
He doesn't smile. He looks past me into the workshop: the banker, the racks, the half-dressed sill I haven't touched since Round One. His eyes stop on the chisels on the floor.
"Your master," he says. "Did he leave you anything? Besides his debt."
There's a lintel's worth of answer to that, and none of it is his.
"He left me a very high opinion of himself," I say. "Is the Guildhall open on Quarter Day, or do I bring it round the back like coal?"
"Open from the morning bell." He writes something in a little book. "Good day, Halloway."
I shut the door, take the tin down from the shelf over the banker and open it.
Three crowns. Two of mine. One from a Drum under a lime kiln.

I pick up a chisel and close my hand on it. The fingers go round. I can see them go round. I can't feel the handle, so I squeeze too hard or not enough, and I don't find out which until it's on the floor again.
After the gallery emptied I stood on that stand and started humming it down into the stone, a Breath's worth at a time. Five ring went to four.

And the thing under the floor, the thing that was waiting? At four ring, it went quiet. Or I went deaf to it. I haven't decided which I'd rather. Either way I stopped humming, because humming down into a floor that's waiting for an answer felt a lot like giving it one.
Held ring doesn't fade on its own. Four is numb hands, and it stays numb hands until I'm back on a stand to Ground it, and the only stand I can get to is under the kiln.
Thirty-five crowns short, and a mason who can't hold a chisel. I need the side a great deal more than I want it.

Training starts with bloom. The walls get beaten before every match, and afterwards the dust settles on every stand and plate and ledge, fine as flour and grey as cold porridge. Somebody has to sweep it. In the Cellar Ring, somebody is us.

Dov sweeps like he's being paid by the flourish. Mrs. Oduya wipes each plate with a cloth and then listens to it, head tilted, the way you'd sniff milk. Marten does the stands on his knees, slow, humming. Sef supervises, which he insists is a job.
I take the doorway at the foot of the stair, because I'm the one who doesn't mind ladders.
The bloom on the lintel is thick as felt. I brush it off, and stop.
There's carving under it. Shallow work, worn soft at every edge by more years than the kiln's been standing. Nobody has cut a lintel this way in my lifetime, or my master's.

Two figures, each on a little square that can only be a stand. A gap between them. Across the gap, a run of wave-marks, cut like water on an old map. And under it all, a row of notches, some deep, some shallow, spaced unevenly, like a tally kept by someone counting more than one thing at once.
I tap the stone either side of the carving out of habit. Sound. Good bed. Somebody chose this lintel well. I don't much like lintels these days, but I can respect one.
"Sef."

He comes and stands under the ladder. Then he keeps standing there. Dov finishes his stand. Oduya finishes two plates. Marten finishes humming. Sef stands with his head tipped back and his mouth a little open, and his pencil goes on moving in the notebook without him once looking down at it.
"Two people," says Dov, leaning on his broom, "standing much too far apart. Terrible formation. That's why they ended up on a lintel instead of in a league."
"Hush, Dov Carrick," says Oduya, without looking up.
"Got it," Sef says at last, and snaps the notebook shut. "I have it."
"Have what?"
"It." He taps his temple, then the notebook, in that order. "Three things. One, it's old. Two, it's about Dampers. Three, I have it."
"That's two things and a boast."
"Interesting," says Sef, and goes off to sweep something.
Finding a coach is Sef's idea. So is where.

"Three things," he says, as we climb out of the kiln into the evening. "One, we have no coach. Two, Hob had no coach, and Hob's..." He stops. "Two is enough. Three, there's an old Damper drinks at the Lime Barrow, has done since before I could carry a tray. Deaf as a doorstep. Face him when you talk; he reads lips."
"Name?"
"Bartholomew Quist."
Nobody has to point him out. Corner table by the fire, alone, a pint half gone. Grey stubble, big hands. Boots on. He watches us cross the room the way you watch weather coming.
He's the man from the stair.
Sef does the talking, slow and square to his face. Kilnyard. The Midwinter Run. No coach, a new Damper, a very good Caller...
"Thank you," says Dov.
...and would Mr. Quist consider...
"No." His voice is too loud for the room and flat as a trowelled wall. Heads turn at the other tables, then turn back. They've heard it before.
"You haven't heard the terms," Sef says.
"Don't need terms, lad."
Two of his fingers tap the table while he looks at us. A little stop-start pattern, round and round, the way some men jiggle a knee.
I sit down across from him and turn my head so my good ear's to the room, which gives him my left side. He leans to catch my mouth.
"Face me, lad."
So I face him. It's an odd feeling, being the one who has to turn properly.
"You were on the stair," I say. "Round One."
"Stair's not the Drum."
"Your boots were off."
"Wet stair. Good boots."
"You flinched before the last note reached me. A full count before."
His fingers stop. Then start again.
"Old men flinch, lad."
Dov, who can't leave a silence alone even if you nail it down, says, "How'd you lose your hearing, then? Ring?"
Quist looks at him for a long moment.
"One bad night. Cup final. Thirty-one years back. My own fault." He drinks. "Go home."
We go home.
Mrs. Oduya walks beside me as far as the kiln corner, where our roads split. She is quiet the whole way, which isn't like her; her quiet usually comes with notes.
At the corner she stops and buttons her coat to the throat.
"Wren Halloway," she says, low. "I was in this city thirty-one years ago. I went to every Cup final in those days." She looks back towards the Lime Barrow's lit window. "I remember no such final."
Then she goes home and leaves me holding it.
Drill night.
Marten teaches Grounding. He does it the way he does everything: slow, warm, and in about nine words.
"Feet down. Both. Flat."
We stand on our stands, all five of us, four of us empty as jugs. Nobody asks about the fifth, and the fifth doesn't say. Nobody throws at anybody tonight; Sef says stance first, ring later.
"Learn it empty," Marten says, "so you can do it full. Then hum. Not at the room. Down."
He shows us. His hum is low and has a tune tucked inside it, something you'd sing to a child who won't settle. It goes down through his stand and I feel it arrive in mine, faint, the long way round.
Dov hums like a man trying to reach the back row of a gallery. Sef hums in numbered bars. Mrs. Oduya hums one exact pitch and looks pleased with it.
My hands are still rag. My feet aren't. So I try to explain.
"Round One. Throw nine. I felt Gorm's lead-in come up through my boots, before it could've reached me through the air. I knew the pitch. That's why I moved."
Dov laughs. Not cruelly; he just can't help it. "Through your boots."
"They're thin boots."
"Wren tastes the bloom as well, I expect. Smells the Peals coming." He spreads his hands to an audience of plates. "Kilnyard's new Damper, friends. Reads notes with ten toes."
Marten watches my mouth while I talk, the way men do across a loud yard, and says nothing.
Sef looks at me a while.
"Interesting," he says. And nothing else.

So I don't tell them the rest. I don't tell them about the thing under the floor, choosing its words. Tonight, with only four ring in my bones and boots on my feet, the floor is only floor, and I'd sound twice as mad describing something I can't show them.
I Ground my own way instead.

You bed a stone by feel. Mortar down, block on, and then you work it, little shifts with the heel of your hand, until it sits and stops talking back. That's what I do with my feet. Heels first. Then the balls. Then I let my weight go down through the stand as if it's the mortar, and I hum one low note, no tune, straight down.
The stand stops talking back. The floor goes still under me, true as a level. One Breath, and a ring goes down into the stone. Four to three.
Something brushes my soles. Footsteps on the stair, coming down. I feel them before I hear them.

Quist stands at the turn of the stair, where the gallery doesn't reach. Uninvited. Boots on. Nobody else has noticed him. He watches me, my feet mostly, for about as long as it takes to Ground one Breath.
Then he turns and goes back up without a word.
"Was that..." says Dov.
"Yes," says Sef.
I keep my feet where they are and hum the rest of it down. Two. One. None. Pins and needles climb both wrists, and my thumbs come back to me like feeling into a cold room.
Under the floor, nothing. Just the stand, and a silence that feels like someone holding their breath.
The drill's finished, and Marten is saying "aye, well" to nobody in particular.
Then the stair talks to my soles again. Heavy boots, coming down. Slower this time. A man arguing with himself on every step.
He comes all the way down this time, to the last step. He stops there, one foot hanging over the Drum floor like it's cold water, and doesn't put it down.

He looks straight at me. No "lad" this time. If anyone in Caddrow knows what my feet are hearing, it's this man, and he's looking at me like he already does. The Drum takes his flat, too-loud voice and lays it at my feet.
"Who taught you to stand like that?"
